Remarks by Jay McEntee:

This recording comes from a collection of Bob Campbell's recordings that were donated to the University of Florida by Campbell's widow, Heather Campbell, in February 2015. See details at: http://www.library.ufl.edu/spec/manuscript/guides/campbell.htm. The recording can also be accessed directly from the University of Florida at: http://ufdc.ufl.edu/AA00050139/. Please contact Daniel Reboussin (danrebo at uflib dot ufl dot edu) with any questions about the rest of this collection. Also note the preferred citation for this material: [Identification of item], Bob Campbell Papers, Special and Area Studies Collections, George A. Smathers Libraries, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida.

Campbell made this recording in the first year (1968) he visited Dian Fossey's Karisoke Camp, which she established in 1967. The tape was labeled "Field recording of gorilla vocalizations, chest beating and other". The recording was included by UF librarian Daniel Reboussin in a display of Campbell's documentation of Karisoke, commemorating the 50th anniversary of its establishment.

The song bout captured in the recording has the form of double-collared sunbird territorial bout singing, with a series of short calls interspersed with silence leading to a ~2 - 5s long complex trill-like component. It seems there are at least 5 possibilities for the source of the song: Northern Double-collared Sunbird Cinnyris reichenowi, Olive-bellied Sunbird Cinnyris chloropygius, Regal sunbird Cinnyris regia, Ruwenzori Double-collared Sunbird Cinnyris stuhlmanni, and Rockefeller's Sunbird Cinnyris rockefelleri. Based on song recordings of the first three on xeno-canto, I do not believe any are a match. I have not been able to find recordings of territorial bout singing, as is heard in the recording, of either C. stuhlmanni or C. rockefelleri. As C. stuhlmanni appears to be common in the Virunga Mountains, whereas C. rockefelleri is not, I suggest C. stuhlmanni is far more likely. According to Cheke and Mann's book Sunbirds (2001), the local race of C. stuhlmanni is C. s. graueri.
